subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Not-for-profit organisations are those which are established not for making profit but-

options.A: to earn a return for their members, and are also called mutual entities
options.B: to trade in goods at cost, and are also called non-profit traders
options.C: to hold property on behalf of the government, and are also called public entities
options.D: to provide some service, and are also called non-trading entities

answer_html:
Answer: (D) to provide some service, and are also called non-trading entities.

There are certain organisations that are not established for making profit but to provide some service, and these services are generally given to members who make subscriptions to avail them. Such organisations are also called non-trading entities, and they are formed for some charitable, religious or similar purposes, their income being spent on the objects for which they are started.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Which of the following is given as an example of a not-for-profit organisation?

options.A: A partnership firm of chartered accountants
options.B: A private limited trading company
options.C: A sole proprietorship retail store
options.D: A gymkhana or sports club

answer_html:
Answer: (D) A gymkhana or sports club.

The examples given are gymkhana or sports clubs, educational institutions, public hospitals, libraries, cultural clubs such as Rotary or Lions clubs, religious institutions and charitable trusts. Each of these furnishes a service to a particular group or to the public at large rather than carrying on business for profit.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The surplus generated by a not-for-profit organisation in the form of an excess of income over expenditure-

options.A: must be refunded to the donors who contributed during the year
options.B: is not allocated amongst the members
options.C: is distributed amongst the members in proportion to their subscriptions
options.D: is distributed amongst the members of the managing committee alone

answer_html:
Answer: (B) is not allocated amongst the members.

Among the salient features of a not-for-profit organisation is that the surplus generated in the form of an excess of income over expenditure is not allocated amongst the members. Such organisations are established and organised as charitable societies or trusts, their subscribers are known as members, and their activities are normally regulated by a managing or executive committee selected or elected by the members.
topic_text: The surplus of a not-for-profit organisation
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The principal sources of income of a not-for-profit organisation are-

options.A: share capital, debentures, secured loans from banks and public deposits accepted
options.B: entrance fees, sales of goods, dividends on trade investments and profit on speculation
options.C: entrance fees, life membership fees, annual subscriptions, donations, grants and legacies
options.D: sales of goods, commission earned, interest on trade advances and discounts received

answer_html:
Answer: (C) entrance fees, life membership fees, annual subscriptions, donations, grants and legacies.

The principal sources of income of these organisations are entrance fees, life membership fees, annual subscriptions, donations, grants and legacies. They are formed not for carrying on a business and making a profit but for some charitable, religious or similar purposes.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The periodic financial statements of a not-for-profit organisation comprise-

options.A: the Receipts and Payments Account, the Income and Expenditure Account and the Balance Sheet
options.B: the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet
options.C: the Receipts and Payments Account, the Trading Account and the Balance Sheet
options.D: the Cash Book, the Income and Expenditure Account and the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the Receipts and Payments Account, the Income and Expenditure Account and the Balance Sheet.

The periodic financial statements comprise the Receipts and Payments Account, prepared to determine the inflow and outflow of cash for a given period, the Income and Expenditure Account, prepared to determine the surplus or deficit for the period concerned, and the Balance Sheet, prepared to assess the financial state of affairs at the end of the accounting period.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Receipts and Payments Account is-

options.A: similar to a trial balance and is a summary of it
options.B: similar to a balance sheet and is a summary of it
options.C: similar to a cash book and is a summary of it
options.D: similar to a profit and loss account and is a summary of it

answer_html:
Answer: (C) similar to a cash book and is a summary of it.

The Receipts and Payments Account is similar to a cash book and is a summary of the cash book. It contains all the cash and bank transactions made by the organisation during a particular financial period, all the entries being made on a cash basis.
topic_text: Nature of the Receipts and Payments Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In the Receipts and Payments Account-

options.A: receipts and payments are both shown on the debit side, the balance appearing on the credit side
options.B: receipts and payments are shown in a single column, the balance being struck at the end of the year
options.C: receipts are shown on the debit side and payments on the credit side
options.D: payments are shown on the debit side and receipts on the credit side

answer_html:
Answer: (C) receipts are shown on the debit side and payments on the credit side.

In the Receipts and Payments Account, receipts are shown on the debit side and payments are shown on the credit side. It begins with the cash in hand and at bank at the commencement of the year and ends with those balances at the close of the year.
topic_text: Sides of the Receipts and Payments Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Receipts and Payments Account and the Income and Expenditure Account are respectively-

options.A: a personal account and a nominal account
options.B: a real account and a personal account
options.C: a real account and a nominal account
options.D: a nominal account and a real account

answer_html:
Answer: (C) a real account and a nominal account.

The Receipts and Payments Account is basically a real account by nature and serves the purpose of a real account, whereas the Income and Expenditure Account is a nominal account by nature and serves the purpose of a nominal account, closely resembling the Profit and Loss Account of a trading concern.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Income and Expenditure Account is similar to-

options.A: the Trading Account and is prepared on exactly the same principles
options.B: the Cash Book and is prepared on exactly the same principles
options.C: the Balance Sheet and is prepared on exactly the same principles
options.D: the Profit and Loss Account and is prepared on exactly the same principles

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the Profit and Loss Account and is prepared on exactly the same principles.

The Income and Expenditure Account is similar to the Profit and Loss Account and is prepared exactly on the same principles. As the name suggests, only revenue items are recorded in it, and both incomes and expenses must be taken on the basis of the accrual concept.
topic_text: Nature of the Income and Expenditure Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: As regards the two sides of the Income and Expenditure Account-

options.A: incomes and expenses are both recorded on the credit side of the account
options.B: incomes and expenses are recorded in the order in which the cash is received or paid
options.C: incomes are recorded on the credit side and expenses on the debit side
options.D: incomes are recorded on the debit side and expenses on the credit side

answer_html:
Answer: (C) incomes are recorded on the credit side and expenses on the debit side.

In the Income and Expenditure Account, incomes are recorded on the credit side while the expenses are recorded on the debit side, all expenses of a revenue nature for the particular period being debited on an accrual basis and all revenue incomes related to the period being credited on the same basis.
topic_text: Sides of the Income and Expenditure Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The excess of income over expenditure and the excess of expenditure over income are respectively called-

options.A: a surplus and a deficit
options.B: a deficit and a surplus
options.C: a net profit and a net loss
options.D: a gross profit and a gross loss

answer_html:
Answer: (A) a surplus and a deficit.

The Income and Expenditure Account shows either a surplus or a deficit. The excess of income over expenditure is called a surplus and the excess of expenditure over income is called a deficit. A surplus is added to the Capital or General Fund in the Balance Sheet and a deficit is deducted from it.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In the Balance Sheet of a not-for-profit organisation-

options.A: there is no capital account, but instead there is a capital fund
options.B: there is a capital account in the name of the managing committee
options.C: there is neither a capital account nor a capital fund of any kind
options.D: there is a capital account for each of the subscribing members

answer_html:
Answer: (A) there is no capital account, but instead there is a capital fund.

The Balance Sheet of a not-for-profit organisation is prepared as on the last day of the accounting period and is based on the accounting equation, but there is no capital account; instead there is a capital fund. The surplus or deficit from the Income and Expenditure Account is adjusted against this capital fund at the end of the year.
topic_text: Capital fund in place of capital
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The capital fund of a not-for-profit organisation is also called-

options.A: the Sinking Fund or the Redemption Fund
options.B: the Building Fund or the Special Fund
options.C: the Reserve Fund or the Contingency Fund
options.D: the General Fund or the Accumulated Fund

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the General Fund or the Accumulated Fund.

The capital fund is also called the General Fund or the Accumulated Fund and is actually the capital of a non-profit concern. It may be found out as the excess of assets over liabilities, and usually the surplus or deficit during a period is added to or deducted from it.
topic_text: Other names of the capital fund

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Money paid to a person invited to deliver a lecture or to an artist invited to perform for the members of a club is-

options.A: termed an honorarium and is added to the Capital Fund in the Balance Sheet
options.B: termed a legacy and is added to the Capital Fund in the Balance Sheet
options.C: termed an honorarium and is debited to the Income and Expenditure Account
options.D: termed a salary and is debited to the Income and Expenditure Account

answer_html:
Answer: (C) termed an honorarium and is debited to the Income and Expenditure Account.

Persons may be invited to deliver lectures, or artists may be invited for their performance, by a club for its members. Any money so paid is termed an honorarium and not a salary, and such honorarium represents expenditure and will be debited to the Income and Expenditure Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A legacy is the amount or other item of value received-

options.A: from the government by way of a grant, and is credited to the Income and Expenditure Account of the year
options.B: from a deceased person under the terms of a will, and is directly added to the Capital Fund after deduction of tax
options.C: from a member on joining the organisation, and is directly added to the Capital Fund after deduction of tax
options.D: from a donor for a specific purpose, and is credited to the relevant Special Fund after deduction of tax

answer_html:
Answer: (B) from a deceased person under the terms of a will, and is directly added to the Capital Fund after deduction of tax.

A legacy is the amount or other item of value received from a deceased person under the terms of a will, and it is to be directly added to the Capital Fund after the deduction of tax, if any. It is therefore a capital receipt and does not pass through the Income and Expenditure Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Receipts and Payments Account records-

options.A: revenue items only, and only those pertaining to the current year
options.B: capital as well as revenue items, but only those pertaining to the current year
options.C: revenue items only, but including those pertaining to the previous and subsequent years
options.D: capital as well as revenue items, and items pertaining to the previous, current or subsequent years

answer_html:
Answer: (D) capital as well as revenue items, and items pertaining to the previous, current or subsequent years.

Entries in the Receipts and Payments Account are made on a cash basis, and items pertaining to the previous year, the current year or subsequent years are all recorded. Capital as well as revenue items are entered in it, all cash receipts of both kinds being debited and all cash payments of both kinds being credited.
topic_text: Items recorded in the Receipts and Payments Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: As regards provisions and other non-cash items, the Receipts and Payments Account-

options.A: records provisions but not notional losses, depreciation being taken to the Balance Sheet directly
options.B: records notional losses but not provisions, the provisions being taken to the Capital Fund directly
options.C: records no provisions at all, and does not record notional losses or non-cash expenses such as bad debts and depreciation
options.D: records all provisions in the same manner as the Income and Expenditure Account records them

answer_html:
Answer: (C) records no provisions at all, and does not record notional losses or non-cash expenses such as bad debts and depreciation.

No provisions are recorded in the Receipts and Payments Account. Being a summary of the cash book, it does not record notional loss or non-cash expenses such as bad debts and depreciation, whereas the Income and Expenditure Account considers all such expenses for matching against revenues.
topic_text: Provisions in the Receipts and Payments Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The opening and closing balances of the Receipts and Payments Account-

options.A: are reflected as assets in the balance sheet, and the closing balance is carried forward to the same account of the next period
options.B: are reflected as liabilities in the balance sheet, and the closing balance is transferred to the capital fund of the year
options.C: are not reflected in the balance sheet at all, being merely memoranda figures of the cash book
options.D: are reflected as assets in the balance sheet, and the closing balance is transferred to the capital fund of the year

answer_html:
Answer: (A) are reflected as assets in the balance sheet, and the closing balance is carried forward to the same account of the next period.

The opening and closing balances of the Receipts and Payments Account are reflected as assets in the balance sheet, and its closing balance is carried forward to the same account of the next accounting period. It is the closing balance of the Income and Expenditure Account which is transferred to the Capital Fund, General Fund or Accumulated Fund in the same period's balance sheet.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Income and Expenditure Account should reflect-

options.A: only those items for which cash has actually been received or paid during the period
options.B: only items pertaining to the current period, previous and subsequent year items being excluded
options.C: items pertaining to the current period as well as to the previous and subsequent years
options.D: only items pertaining to the previous period, the current year items being carried forward

answer_html:
Answer: (B) only items pertaining to the current period, previous and subsequent year items being excluded.

The Income and Expenditure Account should reflect only items that pertain to the current period, previous and subsequent year items being excluded. Only the current year's incomes and expenses are recorded, amounts related to other periods being deducted and amounts outstanding for the current year being added.
topic_text: Period covered by the Income and Expenditure Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: As regards capital items, the Income and Expenditure Account is one in which-

options.A: all capital incomes and expenditures are included along with the revenue items
options.B: all capital incomes and expenditures are excluded
options.C: all capital incomes are included but capital expenditures are excluded
options.D: all capital expenditures are included but capital incomes are excluded

answer_html:
Answer: (B) all capital incomes and expenditures are excluded.

Among the features of the Income and Expenditure Account is that all capital incomes and expenditures are excluded, only revenue items being recorded. It records revenue transactions only, whereas the Receipts and Payments Account records both capital and revenue transactions.
topic_text: Capital items in the Income and Expenditure Account
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: As regards the sale of an asset and the depreciation on assets, in the Income and Expenditure Account-

options.A: the whole of the sale proceeds of an asset is credited and no depreciation of any kind is debited
options.B: profit on the sale of an asset is debited, loss on the sale of an asset is credited and depreciation is ignored
options.C: neither the profit nor the loss on the sale of an asset is recorded, both being taken to the Capital Fund
options.D: profit on the sale of an asset is credited, loss on the sale of an asset is debited and annual depreciation is also debited

answer_html:
Answer: (D) profit on the sale of an asset is credited, loss on the sale of an asset is debited and annual depreciation is also debited.

Profit on the sale of an asset is credited to the Income and Expenditure Account while loss on the sale of an asset is debited to it, and the annual depreciation on assets is also debited. The sale proceeds themselves are a capital receipt and appear only in the Receipts and Payments Account.
topic_text: Sale of an asset and depreciation
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A surplus and a deficit are respectively-

options.A: carried forward to the Receipts and Payments Account of the following year
options.B: added to and deducted from the Capital or General Fund in the Balance Sheet
options.C: deducted from and added to the Capital or General Fund in the Balance Sheet
options.D: shown as an asset and as a liability in the Balance Sheet respectively

answer_html:
Answer: (B) added to and deducted from the Capital or General Fund in the Balance Sheet.

If the income is more than the expenditure it is called a surplus and is added to the Capital or General Fund in the Balance Sheet, and if the expenditure is more than the income it is a deficit and is deducted from the Capital or General Fund. In the format of the account the surplus appears on the debit side as 'To Capital Fund' and the deficit on the credit side as 'By Capital Fund'.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Transactions are recorded in the Receipts and Payments Account and in the Income and Expenditure Account respectively on-

options.A: a cash basis in each case, the difference lying only in the items included
options.B: an accrual basis in each case, the difference lying only in the items included
options.C: a cash basis and an accrual basis
options.D: an accrual basis and a cash basis

answer_html:
Answer: (C) a cash basis and an accrual basis.

In the Receipts and Payments Account transactions are recorded on a cash basis, so that amounts related to a previous period or a future period may remain included and the outstanding amount for the current year is excluded. In the Income and Expenditure Account transactions are recorded on an accrual basis, so that all amounts not related to the current period are excluded and outstanding amounts of the current period are added.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Receipts and Payments Account and the Income and Expenditure Account respectively help to prepare-

options.A: the Income and Expenditure Account and the Balance Sheet
options.B: the Balance Sheet and the Income and Expenditure Account
options.C: the Balance Sheet and the Receipts and Payments Account of the next year
options.D: the Trial Balance and the Receipts and Payments Account of the next year

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the Income and Expenditure Account and the Balance Sheet.

The Receipts and Payments Account helps to prepare an Income and Expenditure Account, and the Income and Expenditure Account in turn helps to prepare a Balance Sheet. This follows the sequence in which the three statements of a not-for-profit organisation are drawn up.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The Profit and Loss Account and the Income and Expenditure Account are respectively prepared by-

options.A: not-for-profit organisations and profit-oriented business undertakings
options.B: manufacturing concerns and trading concerns alike
options.C: companies and partnership firms respectively
options.D: profit-oriented business undertakings and not-for-profit organisations

answer_html:
Answer: (D) profit-oriented business undertakings and not-for-profit organisations.

The Profit and Loss Account is prepared by profit-oriented business undertakings while the Income and Expenditure Account is prepared by not-for-profit organisations. The debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account is known as a net loss and is deducted from the opening capital, whereas the credit balance of the Income and Expenditure Account is a surplus and is added to the opening capital fund.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The capital fund of a not-for-profit organisation may be found out as-

options.A: the excess of income over expenditure for the year
options.B: the total of the subscriptions received since inception
options.C: the excess of assets over liabilities
options.D: the excess of liabilities over assets

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the excess of assets over liabilities.

The capital fund is actually the capital of a non-profit concern and may be found out as the excess of assets over liabilities. Usually the surplus or deficit during a period is added to or deducted from it, and a portion of capitalised incomes such as donations may also be added to it.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A special fund of a not-for-profit organisation-

options.A: may be created out of any source, but the balance of the fund is always shown as an asset in the balance sheet
options.B: may be created out of a special donation or subscription or out of a portion of the surplus, and any income from the investments made against it is transferred to the fund
options.C: may be created only out of the surplus of the year, and any income from the investments made against it is credited to the Income and Expenditure Account
options.D: may be created only out of a special donation, and any income from the investments made against it is added directly to the Capital Fund

answer_html:
Answer: (B) may be created out of a special donation or subscription or out of a portion of the surplus, and any income from the investments made against it is transferred to the fund.

A special fund may be created out of a special donation or subscription or out of a portion of the surplus, an example being a building fund of a club. It may be used for meeting some specific expenses or for acquiring an asset, and if any income is derived out of the investments made against this fund, or if any profit or loss occurs on the sale of such investments, that income or profit or loss is transferred to the fund. The balance of the fund is shown as a liability in the balance sheet.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where a special fund is used to purchase an asset, the entries passed are-

options.A: Capital Fund A/c Dr., to Bank A/c with the cost of the asset, and Special Fund A/c Dr., to Asset A/c
options.B: Asset A/c Dr., to Bank A/c with the cost of the asset, and Special Fund A/c Dr., to Capital Fund A/c
options.C: Special Fund A/c Dr., to Bank A/c with the cost of the asset, and no further entry being required
options.D: Asset A/c Dr., to Special Fund A/c with the cost of the asset, and Capital Fund A/c Dr., to Bank A/c

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Asset A/c Dr., to Bank A/c with the cost of the asset, and Special Fund A/c Dr., to Capital Fund A/c.

Where a special fund is used to purchase an asset, the asset is recorded by debiting the Asset A/c and crediting the Bank A/c with the cost, and the special fund is then closed by debiting the Special Fund A/c and crediting the Capital Fund A/c. Where the fund is used merely to meet an expense, the entry is Special Fund A/c Dr., to Bank A/c.
topic_text: Special fund used to purchase an asset
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A donation received for a particular purpose should be credited to-

options.A: the Receipts and Payments Account alone, no further treatment being necessary at all
options.B: the relevant Special Fund, so that a donation for a building is credited to the Building Fund Account
options.C: the Income and Expenditure Account, whatever the purpose for which it was given may be
options.D: the Capital Fund directly, so that a donation for a building is added to the Capital Fund

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the relevant Special Fund, so that a donation for a building is credited to the Building Fund Account.

A donation received for a particular purpose should be credited to a special fund; for example, a donation received for a building should be credited to the Building Fund Account. For other donations the by-laws or rules of the concern should be followed.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where the rules of the concern make no provision, donations received of a non-recurring nature and of a recurring nature are respectively credited to-

options.A: the Capital Fund and the Income and Expenditure Account
options.B: the Income and Expenditure Account and the Capital Fund
options.C: the Capital Fund in each case, whatever the nature of the donation
options.D: a Special Fund in each case, whatever the nature of the donation

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the Capital Fund and the Income and Expenditure Account.

For donations other than those received for a particular purpose, the by-laws or rules of the concern should be followed, and if there is no such rule, donations received of a non-recurring nature should be credited to the Capital Fund while recurring donations received should be credited to the Income and Expenditure Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A donation paid by the not-for-profit organisation itself is-

options.A: debited to the relevant Special Fund Account
options.B: shown as an asset in the Balance Sheet until it is written off
options.C: debited to the Income and Expenditure Account
options.D: deducted from the Capital Fund in the Balance Sheet

answer_html:
Answer: (C) debited to the Income and Expenditure Account.

A donation paid by the concern should be debited to the Income and Expenditure Account, being an expenditure of the period. This is to be distinguished from donations received, whose treatment depends on whether they are for a particular purpose and whether they are recurring or non-recurring.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where the rules of the concern make no provision, an entrance or admission fee paid once by members for acquiring membership-

options.A: should be credited to a special Entrance Fees Fund and amortised over the expected period of the membership of the member from whom it has been received
options.B: should be shown on the assets side of the balance sheet until the member concerned ceases to be a member of the organisation for any reason whatever
options.C: should be added to the Capital Fund, though if the amount is small and covers only the expenses of admission it may go to the Income and Expenditure Account
options.D: should be credited to the Income and Expenditure Account in every case, since fees of this kind are received year after year from the members newly admitted

answer_html:
Answer: (C) should be added to the Capital Fund, though if the amount is small and covers only the expenses of admission it may go to the Income and Expenditure Account.

As regards entrance or admission fees, the rules or by-laws of the concern should be followed, and if there is no such rule, admission or entrance fees paid once by members for acquiring membership should be added to the Capital Fund. If such fees are of small amounts covering the expenses of admission only, the fees may be credited to the Income and Expenditure Account.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Life membership fees are lump-sum fees collected from new members at the time of their joining, and being non-recurring in nature they may be treated either as-

options.A: a revenue receipt or as a deferred capital receipt
options.B: a capital receipt or as an ordinary annual subscription
options.C: a special fund or as an item of the Receipts and Payments Account alone
options.D: a capital receipt or as a deferred revenue receipt

answer_html:
Answer: (D) a capital receipt or as a deferred revenue receipt.

Life membership fees are lump-sum subscriptions or fees collected from new members at the time of their joining a non-profit organisation, and being a receipt which is non-recurring in nature they can be treated either as a capital receipt or as a deferred revenue receipt. Where treated as a capital receipt, no separate Life Membership Fund is maintained and the amount is added to the Capital Fund on the liabilities side of the balance sheet.
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where life membership fees are treated as a deferred revenue receipt, a separate Life Membership Fund is maintained and-

options.A: a fair portion is transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account every year until the fee is amortised, the unamortised amount going to the Capital Fund on the expiry of the member
options.B: the whole of the fee is transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account in the year of receipt, so that no balance at all is carried forward in the fund to the following year
options.C: the fund is carried forward indefinitely and is never transferred either to the Income and Expenditure Account or to the Capital Fund, whatever may happen to the member
options.D: a fair portion is transferred to the Capital Fund every year, the balance of the fund being written off against the surplus of the year in which the member ceases to be one

answer_html:
Answer: (A) a fair portion is transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account every year until the fee is amortised, the unamortised amount going to the Capital Fund on the expiry of the member.

Where life membership fees are treated as deferred revenue receipts, a separate Life Membership Fund is maintained and the fees received are credited to that fund only. Every year a fair portion of the life membership fee is transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account until the total amount of the fee is amortised, and in the event of the expiry of the member the unamortised amount is to be transferred to the Capital Fund.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The receipts on account of the sale of old newspapers, magazines and periodicals are-

options.A: treated as income and credited to the Income and Expenditure Account
options.B: treated as a capital receipt and added to the Capital Fund
options.C: deducted from the cost of the newspapers and periodicals purchased during the year
options.D: credited to a special fund created for the purpose of meeting library expenses

answer_html:
Answer: (A) treated as income and credited to the Income and Expenditure Account.

As old newspapers, magazines and periodicals are to be disposed of every year, the receipts on account of such sales should be treated as income and are therefore credited to the Income and Expenditure Account. The sale proceeds of used sports material are treated in the same way, the sale being a regular feature of clubs.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where a club runs a restaurant or a bar-

options.A: a separate Restaurant or Bar Trading Account is prepared in the same way as a normal Trading Account and the resultant profit or loss is transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account
options.B: the receipts and payments of the restaurant are shown gross in the Income and Expenditure Account without any separate trading account being prepared
options.C: a separate Restaurant Trading Account is prepared and its profit or loss is added directly to the Capital Fund in the balance sheet
options.D: the whole of the restaurant takings is treated as a capital receipt because the restaurant is not the main object of the club

answer_html:
Answer: (A) a separate Restaurant or Bar Trading Account is prepared in the same way as a normal Trading Account and the resultant profit or loss is transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account.

In order to calculate the profit, a separate Restaurant or Bar Trading Account is prepared in the same way as a normal Trading Account, and the resultant profit or loss is transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account. A similar trading account may also be prepared for any other subsidiary activity, and the surplus or deficit from any other activity is likewise transferred to the Income and Expenditure Account.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
case_facts_html:
An association presents the following particulars for the year. Fees collected were ₹28,000, including ₹3,000 on account of the last year, and fees for the year still outstanding were ₹5,000.

Salary paid was ₹2,400, including ₹300 on account of the last year, and salary outstanding was ₹400. Meeting expenses were ₹2,000, travelling and conveyance ₹800, entertainment expenses ₹500, tournament expenses ₹1,000, rent ₹1,200, postage, telephone and telegram charges ₹1,700 and printing and stationery ₹500.

The purchase of books and periodicals came to ₹3,000, of which ₹2,000 was for the purchase of books. Donations of ₹800 were received and are of a recurring nature. There is no tournament fund.
question_html: Refer to the fourth case scenario. The surplus for the year is-
answer_html:
Answer: (A) ₹19,600.

The expenditure comprises salaries ₹2,500, entertainment expenses ₹500, tournament expenses ₹1,000, meeting expenses ₹2,000, travelling and conveyance ₹800, cost of periodicals ₹1,000, rent ₹1,200, postage, telephone and telegram charges ₹1,700 and printing and stationery ₹500, that is ₹11,200. The income is fees ₹30,000 and donations ₹800, that is ₹30,800, leaving a surplus of ₹19,600. As there is no tournament fund, the tournament expenses are charged to the account.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A club began the year with cash of ₹2,000 and a bank balance of ₹6,000, received subscriptions ₹3,000, donations ₹2,400 and locker rent ₹1,800, and paid for furniture ₹1,600, general expenses ₹1,000, postage ₹400, stationery ₹600 and office expenses ₹800. If the closing balance of cash was ₹7,000, the closing balance at bank is-
answer_html:
Answer: (A) ₹3,800.

The receipts side totals ₹2,000 plus ₹6,000 plus ₹3,000 plus ₹2,400 plus ₹1,800, that is ₹15,200. The payments other than the closing balances total ₹4,400, and adding the closing cash of ₹7,000 gives ₹11,400, so the closing balance at bank is the balancing figure of ₹3,800. The furniture, though a capital item, is included because the Receipts and Payments Account records capital as well as revenue payments.
topic_text: Closing bank balance as a balancing figure

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A club had a building fund of ₹8 lakhs and received a further donation of ₹20 lakhs for the building fund during the year, out of which it purchased a building costing ₹15 lakhs. The amount transferred to the Capital Fund and the balance of the building fund are respectively-

options.A: ₹28 lakhs and nil
options.B: ₹20 lakhs and ₹8 lakhs
options.C: ₹13 lakhs and ₹15 lakhs
options.D: ₹15 lakhs and ₹13 lakhs

answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹15 lakhs and ₹13 lakhs.

The building fund stands at ₹8 lakhs plus the donation of ₹20 lakhs, that is ₹28 lakhs. As the capital expenditure incurred out of the fund is ₹15 lakhs, that amount is transferred to the Capital Fund by debiting the Building Fund A/c and crediting the Capital Fund A/c, leaving a balance of ₹13 lakhs in the building fund, which is shown as a liability.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: On the same facts, if the building purchased had cost ₹30 lakhs instead of ₹15 lakhs, the amount transferred from the building fund to the Capital Fund would be-

options.A: nil, the whole of the cost being met out of the Capital Fund directly
options.B: ₹28 lakhs, the building fund thereafter standing at nil
options.C: ₹30 lakhs, the building fund thereafter standing at a debit of ₹2 lakhs
options.D: ₹20 lakhs, the building fund thereafter standing at ₹8 lakhs

answer_html:
Answer: (B) ₹28 lakhs, the building fund thereafter standing at nil.

The building fund amounts to ₹28 lakhs in all, so although the building cost ₹30 lakhs the transfer to the Capital Fund is limited to the balance available in the fund, namely ₹28 lakhs, after which the building fund stands at nil. A fund cannot be carried at a debit balance, and the excess cost is simply met out of the general resources of the club.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A club had subscriptions in arrears of ₹16,000 and in advance of ₹4,000 at the beginning of the year. During the year it received subscriptions of ₹2,08,000, of which ₹10,400 related to the following year, and at the year end four members had not paid their subscription of ₹1,600 each. The subscription income for the year is-
answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹1,92,000.

To the receipts of ₹2,08,000 is added the opening advance of ₹4,000, which belongs to the current year, and the closing arrears of four members at ₹1,600 each, that is ₹6,400, and from the total are deducted the opening arrears of ₹16,000, which belong to the previous year, and the ₹10,400 received in advance for the following year. This gives ₹1,92,000, and the subscription account totals ₹2,18,400 on each side.
topic_text: Subscription income from a subscription account

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A club received ₹2,000 towards subscriptions during 2022-23. Subscriptions for 2021-22 unpaid on 1.4.2022 were ₹200, subscriptions paid in advance on 31.3.2022 were ₹50 and on 31.3.2023 were ₹40, and subscriptions for 2022-23 unpaid on 31.3.2023 were ₹90. The subscription income shown in the Income and Expenditure Account is-
answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹1,900.

To the ₹2,000 received is added the ₹90 outstanding for the current year, giving ₹2,090, from which the ₹200 of arrears of the previous year received during the year is deducted, giving ₹1,890. To this is added the ₹50 received in advance at the close of the previous year, which belongs to the current year, giving ₹1,940, and from it the ₹40 received in advance at the close of the current year is deducted, leaving ₹1,900.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The subscription credited to the Income and Expenditure Account was ₹3,000. Subscriptions outstanding at the beginning were ₹400 and at the end ₹340, and subscriptions received in advance were ₹100 at the beginning and ₹80 at the end. The subscription actually received in cash during the year is-
answer_html:
Answer: (C) ₹3,040.

The debit side of the subscription account carries the opening arrears of ₹400, the income of ₹3,000 and the closing advance of ₹80, totalling ₹3,480. The credit side carries the opening advance of ₹100 and the closing arrears of ₹340, and the cash received is therefore the balancing figure of ₹3,480 less ₹440, that is ₹3,040.
topic_text: Cash received as a balancing figure

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Which of the following would appear in the Receipts and Payments Account but would not appear in the Income and Expenditure Account?

options.A: The depreciation on the assets, the loss on the sale of an asset and the outstanding rent for the year
options.B: The honorarium paid to a visiting lecturer, the sale of old newspapers and the general donations received
options.C: The purchase of a bicycle, the sale proceeds of investments and a subscription received for the following year
options.D: The salaries paid, the rent paid and the subscriptions received for the current year of account

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The purchase of a bicycle, the sale proceeds of investments and a subscription received for the following year.

The Receipts and Payments Account records capital as well as revenue items and items of any period, so the purchase of a bicycle and the sale proceeds of investments, both being capital items, and a subscription received for the following year, being of another period, all appear in it but not in the Income and Expenditure Account. The items in Option (A) are the converse, appearing in the Income and Expenditure Account but not in the Receipts and Payments Account, since the latter records no non-cash items.
topic_text: Items excluded from the Income and Expenditure Account
